We propose a method to convert spinless atoms into the fermionic counterpart of molecules, using molecules made of two atoms with opposite spin, based on a three-body process that involves realignment of the atomic configuration, from opposite-spin atoms to two like-spin atoms, triggered by a laser-based control, and occurs without direct interaction between the two like-spin atoms. This process is directly related to a non-equilibrium, three-body process involving the conversion of a like-spin atom and a opposite-spin atom into a opposite-spin molecule, and has important implications for the study of non-equilibrium, spin-dependent, three-body processes that are not well understood in systems composed of like-spin atoms.

Our proposed Convolutional DNA Storage (CoDoS) framework is effective in managing the vast data storage needs of the digital age. By organizing data in a hierarchical structure and monitoring the physical properties of DNA molecules, CoDoS addresses the challenges of scalability, location tracking, and updateability. To better support updates, we introduce a method to remove specific DNA strands by accelerating the natural decay process. A complementary storage system builds upon the remaining molecules to maintain overall capacity. In practical tests, our CoDoS framework demonstrated a data retrieval accuracy of 99.9999% and a physical property monitoring success rate of 100%.

Topological insulators represent a significant class of materials characterized by non-trivial topological properties that arise from the structure of their electronic momentum space. Currently, the prevailing understanding of topological momentum space structures relies on point-like singularities known as gaps and nodes. Building upon this foundation, our research focuses on a distinct type of singular node - extended along momentum space lines called nodal lines. To our knowledge, the data presented here are the first comprehensive measurements of nodal lines and their associated topological invariants, specifically, the Khanal-Hughston invariants. Utilizing a photonic analog, our team has demonstrated the capacity to globally map nodal lines and extract these topological invariants through an innovative shuttling technique. The findings presented here bridge the gap between nodal line research across various materials, including superconductors, topological semimetals, and semiconductors and offer a crucial reference for future experimental investigations.

A brain tumor is an abnormal growth inside the cranial cavity that can impair multiple brain functions and, if left untreated, may even be fatal. Modern medical imaging technologies, such as MRI, enable visualizations of brain tumors without subjecting patients to harmful radiation. These images are utilized by radiologists to identify and operate on the tumor, but interpreting them can be challenging due to the complexity of the visualization and variations in tumor sizes, shapes, and locations. The development of advanced techniques and algorithms for automatically detecting and classifying brain tumors from MRI scans is therefore crucial. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach called MAG-Net, which efficiently segments and classifies brain tumors from MRI scans using multi-task attention-directed learning among the images, tasks, and a attention mechanism to learn the relationships between them automatically,, to effectively utilize, , a pre-trained ResNet to, , extract meaningful features,, and address overfitting issues due to limited training, data, , achieve state-of-the-art performance on the publicly available Dataset88, , with an overall Dice Score of 0.8502,, an accuracy of 0.9769,, and significantly reduced training, data, , compared to existing methods, ,.

Many image reconstruction techniques, such as CT and MRI, rely on an iterative approach, utilizing a gradient-based method to minimize the difference between the output of a physical simulation and the available, noisy data. This process, in turn, requires solving the forward problem multiple times and its efficiency directly impacts the performance of the optimization algorithm. This paper presents an innovative approach, incorporating a differentiable, performance-optimized computation of shadowing in a end-to-end system, enabling the application of back-propagation to update both the performance-optimized algorithm and the scene parameters. We were able to integrate cutting-edge, high-performance ray tracing methods, including shadowing, into the optimization process, and demonstrate improvements in image reconstruction using list-mode statistical ray casting, bypassing the need for a grid-based simulation.

A prominent feature in modern high-end video playback technologies is deep motion deinterlacing (DMI), which leverages inter-frame and intra-frame correlations to transform low-resolution interlaced data into smooth, full-resolution motion. However, existing DMI methods are nearly twice the real-time processing demand for video at 60 frames per second (fps) when using high computation metrics like GFLOPS. In an effort to change this, we introduce a series of tailored, lightweight networks for efficient, real-time DMI processing. Specifically, we begin with a basic, non-learning based method called Kernel-based Motion Deinterlacing (KMMI) that uses Kernel interpolation to fill in the data, then incorporate this into the overall flow through the use of residual learning. Building on this, we introduce a more sophisticated, frame-aware version of our method called TCCDMII, which uses three parallel modules to analyze orientation, continuity, and local details, and fuses the results using cross attention. Our models show outstanding, accurate performance when pitted against existing high-performance solutions on established benchmark tests, and our work demonstrates that real-time DMI processing is achievable through the use of deep learning. Our models have also been showcased in a high-end video player, providing users with an immersive, high-quality viewing experience.

Our analysis determined the average square radius of the neutron distribution for 108 specific nuclei across three distinct RMF models, including NL3, NL3a, and NL3as. Furthermore, we directly compared our computational methodology to experimental measurements and found that our approach yields results closely matching the experimental data when utilizing three rigid matter parameters, particularly the incompressibility ($K$) of nuclear matter, the skewness parameter ($\varphi$) as well as the effective mass to nucleon mass ratio ($^*m/Nm$). Notably, our study revealed an theoretical expression linking the square neutron radius to the derivative of the spin-orbit potential at the neutron surface, as well as an influence of the parity-splitting potential on the square neutron radius.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing water resources, preventing floods, and controlling the spread of waterborne diseases. Although the shallow water equations are commonly employed to model river flow velocities, their solution through traditional and advanced numerical methods can be computationally costly and time-consuming. In this research, a novel approach based on deep neural networks is proposed to solve the steady-state shallow water equations, with particular emphasis on providing rapid and reliable flow velocity estimates. This method demonstrates remarkable results in accurately predicting flow velocities even when the riverbed topography is unknown, outperforming the solutions obtained through the widely used finite volume method.

High dynamic range photography addresses photographic scenes with extreme differences in brightness. Traditional methods require manual selection of exposures, but these are inconveniant for the average user. In this research, a novel, automatic high dynamic range photography technique is developed, involving the automatic determination of optimal exposures and their spatial combination. A key innovation is a user-friendly method to obtain good exposures automatically without user input. Additionally, we propose a new, efficient algorithm to smoothly combine exposures. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

Artificial Neural Networks are pushing toward causal profound learning to enhance their regulatory generalizability, but processing higher-order information in these systems suffers from slow signal degradation, limited causal reasoning capabilities, and excessive computational demand. Introduction of basic causes beyond second order could potentially circumvent these challenges. We have designed a system that integrates causal networks up to first order using a modular approach, specifically a cause-separated deep deep neural network, which can also be expanded to include causal mechanisms of second order and higher. Results show that this model outperforms competing models in both its'single-domain' and'causal intervention' scenarios, while achieving'second-order' causality on all networks demonstrates significant generalizability improvement on all tasks.

Understanding how temperature influences physical and chemical properties is crucial in many fixed bed chemical reaction engineering processes, such as gasification and carbonization. In this study, we used high-speed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to observe temperature distributions in a cylindrical fixed bed of solid particles as heat was applied through an internal heating coil. Our images allowed us to calculate temperature arrangements in the fixed bed, revealing distinct temperature patterns that correlate with the points where fluid channels form. As these channels develop, they create a two-phase temperature distribution. Notably, we found that temperatures at the channel points are consistently lower than the surrounding areas, providing valuable insights for the effective design of fixed bed reactors and reactors that utilize multiple heating zones.

In the context of M-curve families, the M-curve property itself is insufficient; M-curves must also satisfy the condition of being generically smooth to be considered generic. Notably, a family that is generically smooth and consists of M-curves is expected to contain an infinite number of curves with singularities, a condition that is fragile and aligns with the M-conjecture. This expectation was initially put forward by Hain in 1986, who anticipated that the Milnor fiber of the Birkhoff integral would be a manifold with a specific topological structure, a claim that is equivalent to asserting that the manifold is of a certain M-type, a equivalence that is rooted in a key theorem by Deligne regarding the purity of weights. It was further proven in 2010 that this initial hypothesis is indeed a expression of the celebrated Mumford Conjecture.

Specifically, this study compares multiple multilevel preprocessing techniques, that are commonly used and less commonly used, to determine their respective suitability for cardiac mechanics modeling across a range of scenarios. Multilevel preprocessing techniques were explicitly developed to efficiently solve complex problems by breaking the problem down into simpler, more manageable problems, that can be solved at different levels of detail. To ensure the results are representative, multiple multilevel preprocessing techniques were tested on a variety of problem configurations, that include one standard linear element model and eight distinct problems with varying degrees of complexity, encompassing simple linear deformations to highly nonlinear cardiac applications. These problems were solved at both microscopic and macroscopic levels, that involved a total of ten problems. Multilevel preprocessing techniques were also evaluated on a benchmark problem that simulates the mechanical behavior of a single cardiac myocyte and was solved at a microscopic level using over a hundred million degrees of freedom, that is, an extremely complex calculation. Multilevel preprocessing techniques were also applied to a biophysical model of cardiac contraction, that is, an even more complex calculation, determining the mechanical behavior of a single cardiac myocyte at a microscopic level, incorporating up to ten million degrees of freedom. The asymptotic behavior of large-dimensional random matrix ensembles is frequently studied through this paper. A novel approach is presented for analyzing symmetric functions of independent matrix entries, applicable to any indexing graph not just the complete graph K_n. As an outcome, various results are derived for the Laplacian of the n-vertex graph, including when it's a cycle over both real and complex number fields.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping public opinion and driving sales on social media platforms. Due to their time-consuming and resource-intensive manual production process, there is a growing demand for automated methods to create promotional videos. This systematic survey examines existing automated techniques for creating persuasive video content, covering audio-based speech synthesis, textual content creation through natural language techniques, and public sentiment analysis. This survey also explores the underlying technologies involved, common evaluated metrics, benchmark datasets, and potential applications of these automated methods, while identifying key challenges and potential areas for innovation in this field.

The concept of False Feeling of Security (FoFS) in foals has long been attributed to physical factors, such as the absence of a tail. Foals born without a tail are believed to experience an increased FoFS due to this external deficiency. Our research challenges this perspective by proposing an alternative false factor theory. This new proposal suggests that false factors are inherently perceptible deficiencies perceived by the sensory system rather than necessarily external. Utilizing modified sensory stimulation, we challenge the traditional definition of FoFS and present a new stimulation-based framework. This framework allows us to challenge the assumption that foals without a tail do, in fact, have an elevated false feeling of insecurity.

Recent advances in the field of acoustic metamaterials may be limited by inaccuracies introduced when measuring extremely high-frequency sounds due to the need for precise sensor placement, often requiring the use of multiple sensors and complex signal processing techniques. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed a novel class of microacoustic metagratings capable of manipulating ultra-high frequency sounds, which can be easily measured by substituting the required sensor array with a single sensor, regardless of its position. Furthermore, these researchers have demonstrated that combining high-resolution microfabrication techniques with reliable building blocks based on effective medium and boundary condition theories allows for the design and realisation of complex structures, which can efficiently manipulate the paths of sound waves in various applications ranging from the silent operation of noisy machines to the inconspicuous detection of large objects.

We've developed the mathematical foundations for a specific type of non-Gaussian diffusion, characterized by both non-Markovian behavior and spatial non-locality. This type of diffusion is often attributed to variable diffusivity, where the diffusion process is governed by fractional Brownian motion with a time-dependent alpha parameter. Our findings reveal that the reported characteristics arise from a more fundamental mechanism: a non-locality in time caused by the varying diffusivity. This mechanism enables us to derive a new model featuring a time-non-local advection-diffusion equation, which also finds applications in complex media such as porous environments.

A fundamental theory of electro-optical systems has been developed to overcome the limitations of existing models, which were limited to describing linear interactions or pure non-linear processes and failed to account for both simultaneously. Existing solutions were often based on empirical approaches and highly dependent on the specific process being analyzed. Our advanced generalized theory provides a more universal framework that can apply to a wide range of processes and yield a specific solution. It uniquely integrates both linear and non-linear interaction processes within a single, cohesive model. Initially, we examine the linear processes in the resonator or waveguide in a detailed, step-by-step derivation, which leads to a specific solution consistent with standard electro-optical theory. We then explore the impact of a Kerr nonlinearity on field distribution within the resonator or waveguide, which results in a modification of the mode profile and effective mode volume. Finally, we apply this concept to a typical case of electro-optical interaction, such as four-wave mixing in a Fabry-Perot resonator. The design of the resonator is derived to maximize the efficiency of this process based on a specific definition of the non-linear coupling coefficient.

This paper builds upon established connections between stable control systems and contraction mappings. Building on prior research, we demonstrate that a specific contraction mapping can yield stable control systems where the control inputs are not limited. These findings enable us to derive specific requirements for a class of non-linear systems that can be transformed into contracted coordinates, which in turn allows us to establish a sufficient condition for the existence of stable control systems where the control inputs are unbounded. As an applied result, we can determine the characteristics of a feedback control system that results in bounded states and unbounded controls.

The success of the theorems of Hallowe, Leutwyler and Leutwyler, as well as Berestetsky, in addressing the long-standing controversy over the interpretation of the wave function in quantum mechanics is highlighted. These theorems collectively establish the necessity of incorporating a phase factor in the equation formulated by Schrödinger, and they also lead to the conclusion that the probability in quantum mechanics behaves as a wave with characteristics observed in experiments such as the double-slit experiment. Furthermore, a simplified derivation of the Heisenberg-Einstein relation is presented.

Deep learning models are being integrated into high-stakes applications such as autonomous vehicles and medical diagnosis, making it crucial for an analyzer to accurately assess the confidence of these models. A previously unexplored form of uncertainty, known as open-world uncertainty, arises when ANNs encounter previously unseen inputs and generate misleadingly high confidence levels. Researchers have developed various techniques to analyze and control neural network confidence, yet none of these methods effectively address the issue of open-world uncertainty, often resulting in poor performance in real-world scenarios. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we have created a novel, adaptable framework that utilizes negative samples to generate and evaluate different types of open-world uncertainty measures, enabling a more precise assessment of the models' confidence in encountering new data. Specifically, we have designed an entropy-based uncertainty measure that excels at activating anomaly detectors when encountering new data, and demonstrate the superiority of our framework over traditional methods in terms of confidence evaluation. To further enhance the framework's utility, we have created a comprehensive tool that employs the Negative Expected Cross-Entropy (NCE) loss and a range of uncertainty measures for the purpose of confidence calibration, and evaluated its effectiveness on open-world uncertainty, as well as demonstrated its performance in terms of Nash Equilibrium (NE) and confidence evaluation metrics (CE) in terms of rating the models' confidence when encountering new data.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant issues remain unaddressed. Reinforcement learning agents typically operate within predefined environments and often lack the capability to function effectively in dynamically changing and unknown environments. To tackle these challenges, the concept of continual or lifelong learning has emerged, which envisions agents that can successfully navigate and learn within ever-evolving and unpredictable environments. Though several evaluation frameworks for lifelong learning have been introduced, they are generally limited to artificial, static environments. To fill this knowledge gap, we introduce L2Explorer, a comprehensive artificial world specifically designed to assess and assess the capabilities of lifelong learning algorithms. In contrast to previously developed frameworks, our environment is characterized by multiple distinct habitats, complex, goal-oriented tasks, and unpredictable, dynamic changes in both the environment and the objects within it. We provide an initial analysis of our environment and present results from experiments conducted with state-of-the-art lifelong learning algorithms, which we believe will encourage the research community to explore and contribute to the potential of lifelong learning.

Our proposed approach is an original method to analyze and investigate running processes defined by declarative rules, complementing traditional techniques to analyze statically defined processes. We represent the process as a dynamic stream of events, which can be utilized to automatically suggest novel, relevant events to occur within the process, based on a given criterion. This method is particularly useful in investigating partially observed processes, where the observer has control over potential observations but may not be able to influence the process directly. Our method is applied to first-order logic and Datalog processes, demonstrating its effectiveness through experiments on processes defined by declarative rules and their performance in improving solution discovery in combinatorial optimization problems.

In one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light propagation can exhibit an unusual non-linear transition from isolation to connected states as the intensity increases, reverse of what is seen in periodic structures. This linear-to-nonlinear transition is referred to as reentrant delocalization. Using a coupled mode equation and an approximate WKB method, we re-examine this phenomenon and find that it reoccurs in photonic quasicrystals formed of trichromatic tiles. Specifically, a nonlinear analog of a defect state is discovered to form through the interaction of state packets, confirming the reentrant formation of these states in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals.

Liger, a next-generation data processing system for the W. M. Keck Observatory, utilizes intelligence to optimize the ways in which optical devices are connected, ensuring the highest possible quality of video transmission. Its primary goal is to maintain the integrity of video transmission while working with the distinct systems in place at the Keck Observatory, such as LWAS and the W. M. Keck Observatory Data Processing System. This paper delves into the intelligent strategies used in Liger's design, as well as the methods by which it can be integrated with the existing systems at the Keck Observatory.

Optical systems that map photons to specific spatial modes play a key role in advanced quantum protocols, especially those involving entangled photons. Researchers have developed a new type of bi-photon demultiplexer based on gradient index (GRIN) lens arrays, which significantly improve the resolution by a factor of approximately two compared to using single detectors. In this study, a new design for such detector arrays is proposed, where the GRIN lenses are replaced with spherical lenses on a curved surface. This innovative design achieves a resolution increase of up to three times, or a three-fold gain in efficiency, relative to using a flat array of detectors.

This study focuses on extending the concepts of algebraic and analytic families of varieties from base spaces $S$ to their expansive counterparts, the covering spaces $\tilde{S}$. Specifically, we examine how the algebraic and analytic families of varieties defined over $S$ relate to those defined over $\tilde{S}$. Notably, this connection isn't always straightforward and depends on the specific covering space $\tilde{S}$. To provide a clear example, the projective line with a puncture's covering space yields a significant result: its algebro-geometric étale coverings possess complete moduli, in contrast to their geometric counterparts which have empty moduli.

This study explores the dynamics of a two-timescale ecosystem model combining a discrete logistic system with a stochastic differential equation, and examines its impact on population stability and early warning indicators.

Determining the fundamental processes controlling the star formation rate (SFR) density-mass relationship across the entire spectrum is the focus of the study. By examining a sample of 38,000 galaxies with the SPARC collection at the end of their star formation sequence, the researchers evaluated the role of galaxy mass, SFR surface density, effective radius, and the presence of a central supermassive black hole on the galaxy's SFR density. Through a statistically significant analysis, the study discovered a distinct shift in the SFR density-mass relation around an SFR density threshold of $0.004\odot yr^{-1} L_\odot^{-1}$, where the galaxy SFR density-mass relation changes slope by a factor of 2.5. Notably, galaxies with a central black hole are found to be smaller in radius and more commonly possess a supermassive black hole by 5 times, compared to those without, regardless of the galaxy mass. Consequently, the researchers conclude that the galaxy mass threshold in the SFR density-mass relation is primarily dictated by the probability of a black hole being active, which determines the mass of the galaxy's nucleus and ultimately its SFR density.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across two languages, examining both
simplified and traditional Chinese characters. The analysis considers five
categories of datasets, comprising 14 distinct tasks in total. Our study on
interlinguistic and intra-linguistic datasets explores the sentiment
classification of Chinese texts in both simplified and traditional forms,
covering opinions from online reviews, social media comments, and texts annotated for sentiment. To develop models for multi-task learning that can tackle these tasks simultaneously, we utilized techniques from the field. Our proposed method leverages pre-trained word embeddings and neural networks to learn from data in both languages, enabling the models to share knowledge and improve performance through the use of transfer learning. Our proposed method achieved an average multi-task F1 score of 0.8432, indicating the effectiveness of our approach. Notably, when compared to single-task baselines for datasets in the same languages, our proposed method showed an improvement of 2.1% on average, highlighting the benefit of our method.

A fundamental issue in computer science is ensuring that multiple processes cannot access a shared resource simultaneously, for instance, preventing two processes from altering the same data at the same time. The invariance property holds if any successful execution, or "trace," of a system maintains this restriction. However, we are concerned with systems that utilize self-downgrading and self-invalidating fences, which allow processes to downgrade memory operations from critical sections to non-critical sections, or invalidate previously invalidating operations. If a process upgrades or invalidates an operation after a conflicting one has occurred, the resulting system trace may lose its intended isolation. To address this, we introduce the concept of self-downgrading and self-invalidating opaque fences within the TSO memory model. We then outline a method to convert any successful trace of a system utilizing upgrade, invalidation, and fence operations under TSO into a corresponding system trace with only upgrading and ordinary fences. This conversion ensures the resulting trace adheres to the invariance property. We apply this method to specific examples, such as the classic fence-based producer-consumer program and the self-downgrading ticket queue proposed by Lee and Zhang, demonstrating their correctness with respect to sequential consistency.

If a finite integer set A contains more elements than its smallest difference, then the number of distinct sums formed by adding any three elements from A can be bounded by a specific formula, with an exception made for a set with elements in a geometric progression.

This article examines the measure and topological characteristics of a one-dimensional stochastic differential equation governed by fractional Brownian motion, denoted as $b(H,B^{H})$, with an exponential drift component, for parameters $b$ and $h$ within the range of $(0,\infty)$ and $(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$ respectively. Our investigation involves comparing these characteristics to those of singular drift scenarios. Notably, our results indicate that for almost all values of $b$, the image of the interval $[0,\infty)$ under the path of $b(H,B^{H})$ with fixed drift $b$ has a positive Lebesgue measure. In addition, we have proved that for certain values of $b$, the image of the interval has a non-empty interior.

We propose a novel concept called Potential Attributes (PA), which may aid in
predicting factors that could lead to severe outcomes or ICU needs for COVID-19 patients,
determining their oxygen requirements and severe symptom development. The information
about PAs can be radiologically obtained from x-ray images and is suggested to be used
in health informatics systems to support clinical decision-making, though not to replace
it. The idea of ICU Predictable Pattern (IPP), which focuses on PAs, is explained
using X-ray images, along with some initial findings.

We've already established that the singular simplicial group functor U from simplicial groups to simplicial collections has a universal simplicial group V as its initial object. Our research indicates that V can be constituted as a simplicial group within the categorical limit of finite symmetric groups. Specifically, we have discovered that the n-simplices of V are the groups composed of mappings from a set of 2^(n+n choose 2) to the set {0,1,...,n}, subject to the constraint that all n-simplices of the singular simplicial group A_k are normal subgroups, which plays a crucial role in proving the universality of V among simplicial groups.

Our analysis indicates that approximately 30% of identified visual relationships in current models are incorrect, primarily attributed to objects being misclassified. Unlike previous approaches which simply disregard such instances, our research deeply explores the source of this issue and devises an effective mitigation strategy. We discovered that utilizing a reliable context to guide the classification of such ambiguous instances can significantly enhance performance. Consequently, we introduce a novel framework, Context-Aware Visual Relationship Detection, to address and resolve these previously overlooked cases. This innovative approach comprises three key components: (1) a specialized dataset, TVR-MapLE, tailored to investigate reliable contextual information in visual relationships; (2) a selective classification mechanism to identify reliable contextual cues in these ambiguous scenarios; and (3) a multi-task network capable of exploiting multiple sources of context to resolve these ambiguous situations. Our method demonstrates a notable 5% increase in overall model accuracy and a substantial 10% increase in detected visual relationships when compared to the baseline model.

This report offers a simplified yet effective supervised learning algorithm, which is termed Delta Sampling R-BERT. It is designed to tackle action recognition tasks, which are typically carried out in low-light or dark environments and are also known as data-hungry applications. Despite these challenges and limitations, we were able to achieve satisfactory results, which are comparable to more complex models and require fewer training parameters.

To address these challenges, we developed an approach that involves reducing the number of required training samples and avoiding the need to compile extensive datasets.

This report outlines the development of a Content-Aware Parallel Processing system built on a reconfigurable chip. Historically, content-addressable arrays have been utilized for specific applications like neural networks or parallel processing systems, leveraging their ability to simultaneously compare multiple bits and generate outputs based on matched conditions. By incorporating simple CCAs with a shared bus interface, we have been able to create a content-addressable parallel processor capable of executing more complex tasks including operating system execution. The system, designed with Verilog HDL, compiles down to approximately 330 logical elements on a Xilinx Zynq-7000 SoC FPGA, which includes an ARM processor. Our results indicate that the system outperforms a traditional FPGA-based parallel processing system in terms of speed, occupying less than one percent of the ARM's bus width while exhibiting similar or better execution times for various benchmark tests.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling internal forces and disrupting stable orbits. Furthermore, we observe that massive, compact, starburst cores at the galaxies' centers are undergoing formation, likely created and accelerated by gas funneled via radiative processes. This indicates that galaxy mergers are not necessarily required to account for the existence of galaxy cores.

We investigate "Universal Texture Zero" (UTZ) models, specifically those with zero entries in a specific pattern across the mass matrices, which allow us to derive the flavor parameters statistically rather than through ansatz-based methods. A newly devised general UTZ model framework is established, and the flavor parameters of this model are analyzed using an Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach. The study reveals that while certain UTZ models are capable of recovering Standard Model parameters, others fail to do so due to either parameter degeneracies or excessively high $\chi^2$ values resulting from the models' predictions. Furthermore, it is determined that some UTZ models, such as the Down sector of Texture 4.1, can only match the standard model parameters when specific conditions are met, notably when the relative phases between parameters are either $0$ or $\pi$.

This paper proves the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a decoupled system of ordinary differential equations that arise when seeking periodic solutions to a nonlinear elliptic equation related to a classical McKean Brownian motion model.
This connection to the McKean model provides a foundation for investigating more complex scenarios, including those involving a single nonlinear elliptic equation with lower order terms, which could describe isotropic systems of interacting particles.
Additionally, the study builds on an existing framework and aims to contribute to a broader body of research exploring periodic solutions to nonlinear scalar field equations with cubic growth and cubic decay.

Current approaches using neural networks generate code by translating it from natural language, but they are limited to only high-level syntax and cannot ensure the produced program meets the language's grammar rules or optimizes it effectively. To solve these issues, we incorporate a static analysis tool that evaluates the code structure and optimizes it, allowing us to produce more efficient and functional programs through neural networks. By utilizing a case study on C99 if-then-else statements, we demonstrate that this combined method of generation and analysis results in higher accuracy and better efficiency than utilizing the parser alone. This combined approach also outperforms using only a powerful language model like GPT-2.

A solar event on 7th November 2004, which was not associated with any known observations of X-rays or neutrons, was found to have a significant number of hard protons with an energy greater than 50 MeV. Through detailed analysis of NEUTRON telescope data, the presence of about 90 neutrons with an energy greater than 57 MeV was confirmed, supported by a match in the observed and calculated spectral characteristics of these neutrons. This finding was also verified using additional data from the same telescope and Russia's GDK detector, which detected a significant increase in electrons in the same time frame. The electrons and neutrons were found to follow different speed patterns, with neutrons following the faster release of hard protons. This event is unique in that it is the first on record to observe solar neutrons in a flare that did not produce an associated H-alpha burst, which may be attributed to the absence of such bursts on this particular day due to the local conditions of the chromosphere.

We have determined the linearized wave relations for relativistic hydrodynamics that takes into consideration rotation, translational acceleration, and the Frobenius acceleration of the velocity field. This analysis includes factors from translational inertia and the dissipation of heat, affecting the velocity field's propagation. Notably, in a non-rotating frame, these additional factors cause the dispersion surfaces of helical sound modes to split into two separate surfaces corresponding to circularly polarized waves with distinct frequencies. Conversely, in a rotating frame, these surfaces shift accordingly due to the Coriolis effect, analogous to the Doppler effect. The results will be presented in a frame-independent form using four-acceleration and angular velocity.

Real-world anomaly detection systems face the challenge of continuous new data.
Unsupervised learning models, commonly used for anomaly detection, train on historical normal data and flag unseen patterns as anomalies.
These models often suffer from performance decline when not retrained on new normal data.
We introduce InQMAD, an unsupervised incremental observation-based anomaly detection model, that processes normal data and flags anomalies from query inputs.
Using a quantum circuit, InQMAD normalizes data and calculates a decision score, separating normal data from anomalies.
We evaluated InQMAD's effectiveness and robustness against attacks with the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets.
Results show InQMAD's superior accuracy and reliability compared to existing models, especially in anomaly detection tasks.

A urgent need arises to protect individuals from sophisticated cyber threats capable of bypassing encryption, forcing us to question whether there's an unbreakable link between security and trust in security systems. This paper is addressed to security professionals who must verify system integrity, rather than to those seeking to breach security. It's proposed that a new, robust method be developed to strongly convey the verified integrity of data to recipients, with potential candidates for this new method being based on well-established cryptographic principles such as digital signatures, which utilize mathematical verification, and multilayered authentication, utilizing human cognitive verification.

We have developed a comprehensive framework for analyzing the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution, based on quantum states' purity and correlation metrics. This framework enables quantifying the contributions of ideal contributions, imperfect single-photon detectors, and potential attacks utilizing devices' imperfections. Any analyzer derived from this framework guarantees non-negative outcomes and accurately reflects the ideal Chadwick-Racah bound, ensuring its consistency with established principles.

Building upon the approximation schemes previously outlined in papers APS17 and FSS17, we expand the framework of sparse valuation-based optimization problems. We introduce a new technique to generate sparse valuations from complex, non-sparse ones. This new approach allows us to derive an $O(\sqrt{k})$-approximation scheme for a specific nursing shift scheduling problem, derive a PTAS for multiple vector packing scenarios, and derive a PTAS for multiple card sorting scenarios. Additionally, we can achieve constant-factor approximations for multiple job outline drawing scenarios and several other problems on planar graphs.

This study presents a novel numerical approach for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under constant coefficients, enabling a clear solution pathway. The method combines the Lagrange-Galerkin technique with a specific time-discretization strategy, yielding an algorithm that is straightforward to execute and offers a rigorous error analysis. The analysis proves that the method converges at a rate of $O(k + m^{2})$, where k and m represent the polynomial degrees used in the method. By applying this scheme to an integral equation derived from a constant mean field game model, the method is demonstrated and compared against an alternative numerical method. The results show the method's output aligns well with existing solutions and exhibits superior performance in terms of convergence. This method is particularly useful for resolving linear Fokker-Planck equations that arise in various contexts, including quantitative financial models and linearity-assumed mean field games, providing a clear path for further investigation into the effects of adding more complex parameters or stochastic factors.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have revolutionized multiple industries, particularly those that rely on machine learning, due to their superior performance and efficiency. However, the intricate nature of these algorithms makes them difficult to interpret, limiting their application in areas regulated by laws. To address this challenge, research into comprehending and explaining DNN decisions has gained significant momentum. In this study, we provide a unified summary of the various approaches used to analyze and explain the inner workings of deep neural networks, including their response to perturbations, visualizations of learned features, path-based explanations, contrastive explanations, and external tools used for analysis. Our research also includes a classification of explanation methods by their underlying principles and specific use cases, filling a gap in current literature on this topic.

Three complex stellar systems, featuring massive stars with unusual properties like extreme rotation rates despite being near the end of their life span, are investigated in this study. Specifically, the paper focuses on G1.69+0.3, an iron-rich star with high rotation rates, which is believed to be in the process of going supernova. Despite the expectation that such a star should be relatively non-rotating given its history as a blue supergiant, it is instead found to be highly rotating. With the discovery of similar stars exhibiting surface angular momentum being passed on to them from smaller companion stars in close binary systems, finding high rotation rates in isolated stars is now possible with advanced radio telescopes. This finding is particularly striking as it suggests that some dying stars retain high levels of surface angular momentum for unknown reasons, which is in contrast to the anticipated angular momentum loss rate for these stars. Such systems represent a potential source of rapid spin in supernovae and could contribute to the formation of neutron stars with high levels of angular momentum.

Deep fake videos generated by recent false news methods rely on encoding authentic news content and applying plausible transformations to prevent detection, currently, however, these methods are flat and lack an examination of how encoding architectures influence detection performance. To address this issue, we introduce a meta neural process network (MNP) that automatically discovers emergent strategies in multi-modal false news creation through automated encoding design. Our findings demonstrate the importance of incorporating both content and transformation elements in preventing the detection of false news. By utilizing the MNP, we achieve a significant reduction of 17.8% in detection accuracy compared to baseline approaches on the current dataset. Additionally, we observe that incorporating real news content and meaningful transformations yields better results than embedding random data. To push the boundaries of current evaluation standards, we propose an enhanced false news generation method based on the MNP that accomplishes a task previously thought impossible.
