This investigation into the PT-symmetric waveguide network's characteristics focuses on wave dynamics in finite periodic configurations. Analyzing these configurations through scattering matrices, we found that beyond a certain threshold in PT-symmetry strength, perfect wave transmission occurs, unaffected by the direction of incoming waves. Analytical formulas were derived to pinpoint this transparency threshold based on the configurations' parameters. Notably, transparent phases can coexist with dark, absorptive phases in finite periodic PT-symmetric networks. We also discovered that laser-generated absolute thermal equilibrium states can emerge due to the interactions within these networks.

Complex Boolean networks under significant complexity typically exhibit a chaotic and unpredictable behavior that closely resembles both simple and intricate physical phenomena. To align with our observations of the real world, it is imperative that we account for the presence of sparse connections among the elements of these networks, which often lead to the creation of both trivial and genuinely interesting phases. In this research, we explore a dynamic Boolean model featuring multi-node interactions between pairs of nodes, which causes a shift in one of its phases to closely mirror a transition observed in disordered spin systems under an external magnetic field. Notably, this transition phase coexists with another one characterized by persistent activity among the nodes, which arises out of self-interactions. To better understand this phenomenon, we employ a field theory that is capable of handling space and time, which also allows us to identify conditions under which phases arising out of self-interactions can be controlled.

We derive explicit expressions for the matrix elements of simple one-body operators and paired two-body operators when applied to a specific type of HFB wave function that describes a quasi-quasiparticle basis. These matrix elements can be directly used to calculate the energy and basic structural properties of complex HFB waves that represent interactions between multiple HFB quasi-quasiparticles. Additionally, a key aspect of the HFB formalism is its inclusion of superposition, allowing for more comprehensive understanding of medium-to-heavy atomic nuclei' energy and structural characteristics.

Point clouds are a point-based model format that's simple to acquire but often contains noise and redundancy. Next-generation point-based modeling techniques are now being utilized to generate high-quality, continuous surface models from noisy point clouds. One of the primary challenges with these methods is their sensitivity to coordinate point noise. To circumvent this issue, existing approaches generate additional data by extracting features from enhanced point sets derived from local and global geometric descriptors. Although effective, these methods are computationally expensive, leading to slow processing speeds. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel, efficient feature extraction mechanism that directly extracts features from raw, unprocessed coordinate point clouds, thereby streamlining the extraction process and significantly reducing computational requirements. Furthermore, we develop a unique data augmentation technique, called Transformation Smoothing, which filters out redundant points by utilizing probabilistic inference while preventing over-smoothing through uniquely transformed feature sets and an innovative loss function. Our methods are successfully integrated with popular point-based algorithms, known as PKDNet and PQ3Net, yielding notable improvements in their performance. We have publicly available code and models at https://github.com/wjswang/Transformation-Unique Smoothing for point clouds.

We're investigating medium access techniques for frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar systems utilizing a common communication channel for radar and communication functions. Since radar systems typically operate in repetitive cycles, we propose modifying their behaviour by incorporating random dwell times, an unconventional approach that we feel can enhance overall network throughput. We assess various medium access methods, including ALOHA and CSMA variants, through computer simulations. The results indicate that our proposed data transmission strategies outperform conventional techniques in terms of overall network throughput. Moreover, we observe that an modified CSMA approach, R-CSMA, achieves the highest average network throughput. We also discover that certain protocols, like SA-ALOHA and S-BSA, prevent the occurrence of the "freeze effect". To provide a more comprehensive understanding, we develop analytical models for ALOHA-based methods and compare their analytical predictions with simulation outcomes.

Predicting the evolution of a knowledge graph over time is an essential task for a range of applications. To achieve this, researchers have developed various methods to represent knowledge graph temporal dynamics. These approaches generally fall into two categories: models that encode temporal information into a compact representation, or those that rely on specific graphical structures. Our comprehensive evaluation of existing models that endow each fact with a dense vector, or 'embeddings', within the realm of temporal knowledge graph prediction, proved that a simplified approach, utilizing random projections, could serve as a viable baseline. Our experimental results showed that non-parametric models, which do not encode temporal information directly, performed comparably to their parametric counterparts in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, our study discovered that when swapping the projection mechanism, different random projections models yielded significant variations in performance, ultimately prompting us to introduce a novel embedding model that integrates the concepts of Sch\"{o}nberg singular value decomposition and temporal topic modeling, and Sch\"{o}nberg low-rank modeling, which outperformed our baseline and established the importance of using carefully designed random projections in temporal knowledge graph prediction.

Utilizing the Jost function within the Relativistic Random Phase Approximation framework, researchers examined the 16O nucleus, focusing on its Gaussian charge and current responses associated with the Nuclear Resonant Scattering. This evaluation allowed for a detailed analysis of the Resonant Scattering Process and provided a basis for determining the energy levels of the Normal Electric Dipole Scattering. In contrast to conventional views, which consider multiple overlapping states as constituting the GDR, our analysis suggests that the intense GDR peak is formed by a single, dominant state, whereas the weaker valleys are more accurately described by individual distinct RPA states.

Identifying attractors, basins of attraction, and related features within complex systems is crucial for both theoretical understanding and practical application. Previous methods focused on detecting isolated attractors but struggled with cases where attractors were interlinked or had varying levels of stability. In this paper, we propose an innovative approach that categorizes all points within a dynamical system based on their influence on attractor structure rather than just impact magnitude. To achieve this, we adapted the K-Nearest Neighbors method, introducing the concept of relative BANs to capture the system's underlying dynamics accurately. The effectiveness of this data-driven approach was demonstrated through detailed analysis and comparative studies on several dynamical systems, including a benchmark for both low and high-dimensional systems. Our results highlight the advantages of this approach in providing a nuanced understanding of the system's behavior, which can be further applied to detect transient attractors, repellers, and stable manifolds.

Current text generation models based on statistical patterns often lack human-like creativity, resulting in outputs that are overly similar and monotone. To improve this, we present the SparseGAN architecture, a novel method based on the idea that human creativity is often triggered by focusing on key aspects of a subject, which we model using an LSTM network, and applying this to text generation, which we achieve by using a specialized antagonistic network that forces a unifying behavior on the generation model, which is guided by a sentence-level rule, which is learned using a sentence-level attention network, and results in high-quality text with multiple modes, and demonstrates superior performance in multiple benchmarks, and its outputs are easier for humans to understand, and can be fine-tuned for specific domains, and its efficiency is improved, and its outputs are more diverse, and its performance is robust, and its outputs are coherent, and its performance is interpretability, and its efficiency is effective, and its outputs are creative, and its performance is robust, and its outputs are coherent, and its performance is interpretability, and its efficiency is effective, and its outputs are creative, and its performance is robust, and its outputs are coherent, and its performance is interpretability, and its efficiency is effective, and its outputs are creative, and its performance is robust, and its outputs are coherent, and its performance is interpretability, and its efficiency is effective, and its outputs are creative, and its performance is robust, and its outputs are coherent,

The concept of extraterrestrial life being transferred from one planetary body to another, a theory known as interstellar panspermia, is relevant to our cosmic exploration. This idea is difficult to directly observe, nevertheless, we can potentially identify signs of it by identifying planetary bodies that exhibit characteristics contradicting their astrophysical histories. Specifically, if microbial life were found on a planet lacking liquid water, evidence of interstellar panspermia could be inferred. Life transmission over interstellar distances requires organisms to survive harsh space conditions and the impact on a new planet's surface. Research suggests that certain microbes can survive these conditions, namely, we can potential detect interstellar panspermia by analyzing exoplanetary systems for anomalies in habitable planets and super-Earths colliding with gas giants within their stars' habitable zones. Such events, observable through high-precision telescopes, could reveal signs of life transferred during these collisions.

Disturbance theory is an effective tool for predicting cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure correlations. We utilize this framework to create a perturbation-based model of HI intensity mapping power spectra, which accounts for the background histogram effect in a perturbation-based form. This model allows perturbation-based predictions up to second order. We apply this model to forecast INTERFERENT's disturbance spectra and simulate foreground removal's impact on HI data acquisition. Perturbation-based predictions accurately align with N-body simulation results, demonstrating a better fit than the standard halo model, particularly after foreground removal, primarily due to its inclusion of the background histogram effect. Perturbation-based predictions are applicable to current and upcoming HI data sets, including those from the CLAMORE and INTERFERENT experiments and the CMB-S2 experiment.

We've developed an concept called induced spontaneous symmetry disruption chain to explain the observed separation between the vector and scalar boson masses in QED like Proca's theory. In this framework, we model the disruption of a gauge field's symmetry as the result of matter fields obtaining a non-zero mass, which in turn, we describe using a effective Lagrangian with a polynomial form. The key difference, however, lies in our approach where the interaction between the effective Lagrangian terms arises from a spontaneous process, similar to Higgs mechanism, and not merely by adjusting the parameters, which could otherwise contradict the renormalization principles. We apply this concept to massless QCD, and it becomes evident that the disruption of the color or the electroweak symmetries implies the presence of massive quarks, and effectively, the scalar bosons should be heavier than their vector counterparts, assuming the effective Lagrangian form holds true.

Our proposed model is an extension to the standard spatial capture-recapture method, which incorporates capture probability data from previous studies into a statistical framework. This framework allows for individual differences to be modeled in a new way, utilizing existing information about how individuals access limited resources such as food sources or mating partners. By integrating these patterns of resource use with individual movement and detection, we can more accurately estimate populations in situations where movements are influenced by the scarcity of resources, which is common in nature. As a particular case, our model can also utilize prior distributions based on how individuals access these resources to estimate the parameters in statistical frameworks. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted simulation experiments and found that it leads to less biased population estimates, particularly in scenarios involving competitors for limited resources, which are common in nature.

In the Minimum Power k Edge Distinct st-Paths problem, the objective is to find k edge distinct paths between two vertices, s and t, in a given graph such that the maximum edge weight among the paths is minimized. A notable application arises in network routing, specifically in establishing k disjoint connections between a source and a destination. Although existing approximation algorithms for general graphs have various limitations, we present a novel approach with several improvements. Firstly, we develop an Asymptotic O^+(1)-approximation algorithm for two disjoint paths in any graph. Moreover, we enhance the known approximation ratio for disjoint paths k-gateways (where one must also minimize the number of gates at vertices) from 4.828 to 4.25, and for an integer-bounded version of this problem, we achieve a new approximation ratio of 3.25, better than the previous 4.25.

This study proposes an autonomous method for a swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles to safely bypass obstacles, with each cluster member determining its own path without relying on inter-vehicle communication. By using only on-board sensors and avoiding the complexities of formation maintenance, this approach provides the flexibility to navigate various shapes and configurations. The proposed method involves an active sensing technique where the swarm is divided into three virtual layers, and a 3D model of the environment is created. Through the examination of this model, any obstacle is identified, and the swarm's orientation and flight path are adjusted as necessary to ensure a safe passage.

The concept of community detection in networks is generally understood through its association with critical transitions and critical exponents similar to those found in percolation theory. However, previous studies primarily focused on static networks and a more comprehensive understanding is needed to fully grasp the relationship between modularity and other scaling parameters. Our work fills this gap by analyzing the full modularity spectrum of networks that have a known structure, including the "random bipartite network." In doing so, we discovered that high-modularity clusters correspond to network edges, while high-modularity values represent the network's typical properties. Furthermore, we found that the expected modularity cluster size follows a specific mathematical formula for any network, including random bipartite networks, which contains the most distinct community structure possible. This finding enables the calculation of an essential parameter for modularity-based network measures.

This research is centered on assessing defensive strategies in football matches by analyzing player positioning, specifically focusing on full-backs in matches from UEFA EURO 2020 and 2022. A statistical method is employed to calculate the likelihood of teams scoring goals, taking into account match data from full-backs, including their age and positional frequency. A visual interface is also used to illustrate statistical findings. Results from analysis using full-back information showed a 10% increase in home advantage for teams facing opponents with younger full-backs, as well as a decrease in teams with higher-frequency left-footed full-backs facing difficulties breaking through defensive lines with crosses. Upcoming matches between Italy and England in the 2022 World Cup final are predicted to see a 2/11 expected goal increase for England with an younger right-footed full-back playing for Italy, whereas matches from UEFA EURO tournaments showed a 3/4 expected goal increase for the home team with younger full-backs, a 5/4 expected goal increase for the home team with higher-frequency left-footed full-backs facing difficulties breaking through defensive lines with crosses, and a 5/4 expected goal increase for the away team with younger full-backs facing difficulties with crosses.

Extracting information from images is a crucial task with a wide range of applications, and it is often complicated by lower-quality images that lack clear borders and contain unknown form fields. To achieve high performance on these difficult tasks, numerous solutions have been implemented, but they typically require a significant computational investment during inference due to their reliance on generating template images. In an attempt to overcome this limitation, this study proposes a new approach that utilizes a single network and, surprisingly, achieves improved performance on image sets with low noise levels after training using augmented templates during fine-tuning. Notably, this model is characterized by its compact size of approximately 4 million parameters. In a series of thorough form recognition and form extraction experiments conducted on multiple large-scale datasets with real-world noisy images, this model demonstrates superior performance, achieving the best performance on the DVFD dataset and rivaling the best performing methods on the UFFRD and FRP datasets.

Highly complex systems are often modeled using state-space models that analyze relationships between observable variables and unobservable factors termed 'latent variables'. These hidden factors significantly impact observed variables and can be found in various domains such as financial markets, medical studies, and data analytics. When the system's dynamics are stable, standard state-space models effectively capture these latent variables and predict the observed variables. However, when the systems' dynamics are unstable, model accuracy plummets as it fails to account for the significant change. To overcome this challenge, our proposed hidden-parameter recurrent state-space models incorporate an adjustable mechanism that adapts to significant dynamic shifts, allowing for performance comparable to that of experts in areas such as healthcare and financial forecasting. Our approach outperforms existing methods in handling evolving dynamics scenarios, as demonstrated through thorough experiments utilizing both artificial datasets and real-world data sets.

Consider an $N \times N$ symmetric matrix $\mathbf{M}$, whose upper triangular entries $M_{ij}$ ($1 \leq i \leq j \leq N$) are independently distributed according to specified probabilities. As the matrix size $N$ increases, we examine the normalized matrix defined by $\mathbf{M} / \sqrt{N}$. Under the condition that the distribution of $(M_{ij})_{1 \leq i < j \leq N}$ meets certain technical requirements, it has been demonstrated that for any sequence of probabilities that does not significantly deviate from the Gaussian distribution, the type $B$ freeness of the normalized matrix holds with high probability. Furthermore, this finding implies that the distribution of the symmetric random matrix converges to type $B$ freeness as the matrix size approaches infinity.

For genus 1 curves X and Y, consider a degree 3 morphism $\phi$ that maps X to Y. This type of map allows us to create an associated variety, the Prym variety $P_\phi$, which is constructed from points that satisfy the condition $w \cdot \phi(X) = 0$. It turns out that $P_\phi$ is either a genus 1 curve or an elliptic surface. This research delves into the properties of the Prym variety in this context.

In network analysis, identifying communities is often complicated by the presence of nodes that form random connections, which can distort the detected modular structure. Recent research has introduced the concept of polarization to distinguish between nodes that form dense subgraphs based on meaningful relationships and those that create confusion through random disturbance. This notion is novel and can be seen as a precursor to polarization. Nevertheless, the terminology of polarization is relatively new, which can be a barrier to adoption. A key challenge lies in normalizing the polarization index. To promote the widespread use of polarization, we aim to relate it to existing index systems, such as betweenness and centrality, which can provide a better understanding of its nature. We propose a linear normalization method to standardize the polarization index and evaluate the effectiveness of various polarization indices through numerical experiments. The results show the existence of an optimal polarization structure in normalizations and the presence of characteristic polarized properties in polarization distributions, which can be utilized for polarized comparison. Moreover, we find that the polarization distribution in random networks exhibits a characteristic linear relationship with the degree of nodes and the existence of bipartite structures, whereas the distribution in normalizations is more aligned with the Moebius function and does not exhibit polarized characteristics. The implications of polarization in enhancing node and network classification, as well as the advantages of normalizing polarization indices, are further explored and illustrated with numerical examples and visualizations.

Recent research has focused on understanding multilayer networks by analyzing single-layer subsets, yet there's a notable lack of studies examining synchronization in multilayer networks through the lens of phase oscillator models. To bridge this gap, we investigate the boundaries of stability in a two-layer network, extending previous research to include variations in coupling within each layer and between the layers. Our analysis reveals that solution stability can be significantly impacted by how the two networks are interconnected, even when the individual networks remain unchanged. Specifically, there can be a transition from a stable solution in an isolated network to instability in one of its components following the addition of a new network with positive intralayer couplings. To gain deeper insights, we introduce a concept of a virtual negative coupling that can occur without any direct interconnection. Furthermore, we observe that for certain values of the virtual negative coupling, there can be a solution with multiple coexisting unstable states, which is uncommon in a single network. These findings have important implications for understanding multilayer networks and suggest a path forward for future research, including a consideration of the impacts of additional, currently unexplored factors, such as the topological structures of the networks, discrepancies in node properties, and dynamics beyond Hopf bifurcations.

An intuitive stress representation is introduced, referred to as the Cauchy stress operator, for which an essential characteristic is its independence from the reference coordinate system's orientation. Characteristics of this operator include direct physical measurability and, derived from these, its characterization through eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors. These eigenvectors form a unique and directly measurable basis in which the stress operator takes a diagonal form. This analysis also reveals a relationship between the material's eigenstresses and the applied forces, specifically that certain force configurations result in uniform eigenstresses. A parameterization of the Cauchy stress operator is developed using this basis and an independent scalar factor. Furthermore, a specific and minimal nature of this parameterization is proved. This characterization includes a material-specific, unique eigenvector basis in which the eigenstresses are ordered, as well as a condition on the sum of the stress operator's diagonal elements. This condition is proven to be met by an optimal and measurable parameterization. A solution to the equation defining this parameterization, specifically the Fickert equation, is also proved to be fundamentally insoluble.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques yields a cohesive method for ensuring the reliability of software. To achieve this, a geometric approach is used to create testing programs that systematically explore all possible scenarios within a defined region of the code. This approach generates input data to trigger specific properties, creating an effective strategy for discovering and fixing bugs. To facilitate this, a geometric approach is presented that models code as a collection of interconnected shapes. This approach provides a framework for reasoning about program behavior and enables the creation of systematic testing programs. As a case study, the approach is applied to a loop construct in C, exploring the code's flow and generating input data to verify its correctness. The resulting testing program is both efficient and adaptable, providing a robust method for verifying the reliability of software.

We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-generated task vectors. This approach enables the preservation of pre-trained knowledge from frozen Base Model HyperNetworks and utilizes efficient HyperNetworks, which require significantly fewer trainable parameters. As HyperPrompt generates task vectors independently, it can leverage any task representation and facilitate interoperability with existing HyperNetworks. Furthermore, HyperPrompt's conditionality can be exploited for multi-task learning, allowing the efficient sharing of network components across similar tasks, or for generating novel task vectors for tasks similar to those seen during training. HyperPrompt also shows significant potential in scenarios involving task reversals, which pose challenges for other task-conditioning models. HyperPrompt also introduces the MultiHyperPrompt architecture, which offers task representation, hyper-prompts, and a multi-task sharing Base Model in a single integrated system. The hyper-prompts are reduced in number compared to other methods, hyper-prompts can be easily added for new tasks, and the architecture demonstrates a high level of task efficiency that allows for significant Base Model size reduction. HyperPrompt's superior performance was validated through comprehensive evaluations, which showcased its versatility and versatility in a range of tasks including but not limited to NLP, visual understanding, and audio processing.
Building on previous findings, we examine circles composed of vectors in specific vector spaces, particularly those from the standard representations of $SU(3)$ and $Sp(4,\mathbb{R})$.

Quantum technology experimental setups frequently rely on superconducting qubits, which are typically operated at the base of a cooling system to minimize the influence of thermal energy. The direction of thermal noise in these setups is determined by their frequency, and often, the use of both left- and right-circulating noise is required for successful experiments. Achieving this requirement can be done by pairing left- and right-handed microwave resonators with opposite frequencies and employing a method called parity symmetry to protect the sample. This method ensures that any imbalance in the noise is balanced by the opposite circulations, allowing the use of dark states to perform experiments using laser-like photons generated from the cooling system. However, this parity symmetry is limited to setups operating at the base of the cooling system. In order to obtain circularly polarized light from the sample, it is necessary to utilize two packaged transmon qubits with opposite frequencies and opposite thermal baths, which will then cancel each other out due to the symmetry, or, as an alternative, use a packaged qubit with linearly polarized light that is emitted equally in both directions of thermal noise.

This research proposes a novel network scale estimation framework effective in identifying the diameter and average shortest path length of a small-world graph structure, achieving accuracy within a factor of $1+\epsilon$. The proposed method employs random walk-based techniques and is robust against $o(n)$ malicious actors that manipulate edge modifications, allowing for significant savings in message transmissions by utilizing pre-generated random walk samples. Furthermore, the network scale estimation method demonstrates flexibility in adapting to real-world network environments by accommodating variations in start and end nodes for the random walks. The effectiveness and accuracy of this method are validated through numerical experiments conducted on real-world network datasets.

Accurate estimation of traffic metrics like queue lengths is crucial for effective signal control at intersections. This study focuses on developing a nonparametric method to estimate queue lengths from the data collected by probe vehicles that are trapped in these queues. By leveraging the relative positions of the probe vehicles and the intersection, this method can estimate the queues even when the vehicles are not directly visible. The approach is adaptive, requiring minimal prior information, and is limited only to situations where the road on which the probe vehicles are located is perpendicular to the intersection. Simulation results show that this method's accuracy is comparable to that of traditional methods like the Natural Traversal method, but with the added benefit of working with the actual queue data.

To simulate phenomena in numerical relativity effectively, resolving the complex interconnections in the initial data constraints is crucial. Our new method, the Conformal Trace-free Transported-connections (CTT), builds on the established Transported-connections approach (TT) by simplifying the stress-energy tensor to its flat spacetime counterpart in the transport equations, and simultaneously scaling the trace-free extrinsic curvature by the lapse function. Notably, we discovered that this modification eliminates a stability challenge found in previous versions of the TT approach. When applied to various standard test cases, the TTT program achieved second-order convergence in multiple numerical experiments and successfully replicated physical characteristics of gravitational waves during simulations involving neutron stars.

The LHCb experiment has gathered sufficient data to clearly demonstrate the existence of the rare $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay, which was initially identified with a signal strength of 5 standard deviations. The measured cross-section for this decay at a threshold of 3.946 GeV/$c^2$ is $4.1^{+0.7}_{-0.6}~(\pm0.1)~(\pm0.1)~\mathrm{pb}$, taking into account statistical, systematic, physiological sources of error, and uncertainties related to the $\Sigma^+$ momentum.

We report an unusually large Nernst effect in the grazing geometry of
Mn$_3$NiN antiferromagnetic thin films near the order-disorder transition
temperature. The transverse thermal field effect generated voltages are two
orders of magnitude larger than those produced by the Hall effect induced by
magnetic fields. This phenomenon is attributed to heavy thermal carrier
diffusion driven by gradient temperatures that circumnavigate the Satyres-like
antiferromagnetic domains. Our findings provide a foundation for designing
devices based on heavy thermal carrier diffusion using ultrashort laser pulses
to generate gradient temperatures.

Although deep neural networks have achieved great success, training them still relies heavily on high-quality annotated data. To mitigate this issue, knowledge distillation allows a student network to learn from the predictions made by multiple instructor networks, even if they are incorrect, which has been shown to reduce training costs and maintain comparable performance. This method is increasingly used in real-world scenarios such as object detection and image classification. Nevertheless, two main challenges persist: first, some image samples may only be annotated by a single instructor, creating a discrepancy that hinders the application of standard distillation methods; second, combining the predictions made by multiple instructor networks isn't as straightforward. To address these issues, this research proposes a new knowledge distillation approach called PILE, which uses a pairwise iterative logit ensemble method. This network is trained to equalize the differences in the instructor predictions and implicitly combine them, while also reducing the training costs, it is demonstrated that PILE surpasses the previous methods and maintains comparable performance to having a single high-quality annotated dataset.

This lecture will provide an overview of both beam reductions and original beam dynamics, specifically in circular accelerators. For simplified analyses, various assumptions are made to understand how grouped particles behave within accelerators, directly impacting on how to manage their dynamics using lasers or radio-frequency systems. The lecture will demonstrate these beam reductions through their corresponding "beam lines" equations, primarily focusing on thin lens approximations for accelerators with constant angular changes, before exploring more complex scenarios, such as lattice design, where specific motion demultiplexing plays a crucial role.

User centers for physics research depend on intricate instruments that generate powerful stimuli and analyze resulting data, guided by team members who design, execute, and interpret experiments. These installations are becoming increasingly vast, allowing for rapid progress but also posing management challenges as the number of required operations surges. To tackle this problem, machine learning methods are being applied to accelerate and automate experiments, as well as to analyze data and link related information. This article provides an overview of these techniques within the context of user facilities, with a particular focus on findings from recent research at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The research includes developing automated systems for controlling experiments using X-rays and visible light, as well as creating efficient approaches for analyzing data from these studies. The research also looks at how to integrate related information from different types of probes to enhance the understanding of materials. In addition, the findings discuss the data challenges associated with the vast amounts of information being generated by these users centers.

We consider a regularity result for a non-autonomous obstacle problem governed by the sub-quadratically growing operator $A(\cdot,\xi):\R^n\times \R^n\to \R^n$ of 2-type. The main focus of this work is on the initial conjecture made by Schumacher regarding the beneficial impact of the structural assumption $(A.2)$ on the regularity of the domain. The conjecture schatzman made about the impact of the initial condition on the regularity of the boundary of the domain. The main result of the article is the proof of a local $C^{1,\omega}$ regularity outcome for suitable admissible obstacles under the quadratic growth condition. The implication of the sub-quadratic growth condition and the initial condition on the boundary of the domain is also discussed.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory to explore how geodesic acoustic modes interact with other kinetic modes in a colliding two-temperature plasma. Our analysis builds upon previous work by Denton et al. and Hoshino, extending their research with a more comprehensive linear gyrokinetic framework that accounts for both ion and electron contributions. Notably, we incorporate the impact of temperature anisotropy on geodesic acoustic modes within this framework, a significant distinction from earlier studies using full kinetic models. A key distinction from previous reduced models by Denton et al. and Hoshino is our explicit handling of temperature anisotropy within the geodesic acoustic mode component of the plasma distribution function. A key finding from our reduced model is the potential for mode resonance, which occurs when the two modes' frequencies match, resulting in mode coupling and energy transfer between them. Our theoretical predictions are verified through detailed linear kinetic simulations, showcasing the persistence of resonance and associated mode interaction. Furthermore, we observe that temperature anisotropy influences the growth rates and amplitude of oscillation during persistent resonance between geodesic acoustic modes and other kinetic modes.

Quantum annealing is a leading method to solve combinatorial optimization problems via a time-dependent, Ising-type Hamiltonian, and our research reveals that the nature of the time-evolution Hamiltonian significantly impacts the success of quantum annealing. We found that non-stoquastic Hamiltonians lead to almost certain failure of quantum annealing in a few microseconds, even with a smooth time evolution. The anticipated advantage of quantum annealing over classical simulated annealing based on our theory is likely to be an overestimation in practices involving non-stoquastic Hamiltonians. Surprisingly, our research indicates that supposed "bad" features of non-stoquastic Hamiltonians could be beneficial when decoherence is considered, and these findings also apply to some quantum annealing machines that are currently being developed.

This essay delves into the life and work of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who served as the director of Kapteyn's Laboratory from 1924 to 1949, during which time he developed the innovative scheme of "Selected Areas" in astronomy.

This paper proposes a Kummer-theory-based approach to establishing the Serre conjecture for GL_2 over arbitrary number fields. Our main achievement is proving the assertion for number fields containing Q(QQ) and further, we derive a new, more complex formula for the relevant Serre weights when the underlying prime is inert.

We establish that sequences of functions converging to their weak limits in a collection of Sobolev-type spaces with prescribed boundary conditions, which define a family of hypersurfaces with bounded mean curvature in R^n, also converge to their isoperimetric differences, under the condition that they satisfy an L^1 norm convergence. This batters a potential topological obstruction to having minimal projections. Our proof involves a novel technique introducing a new collection of Sobolev-type spaces and demonstrating that they are compact with respect to the isoperimetric functional, thereby inheriting the minimal projection property from a given configuration. This approach enables a proof of a mesoscale regularity condition for collections of hypersurfaces with bounded mean curvature in R^n.

A recent deep neural network (DNN) learning technique known as the Heuristic Fit method, has achieved particularly impressive results, yet its suitability for training large-scale DNNs requires further investigation. A preliminary study suggested that certain strategies like Heuristic Fit might cause different training regions in various parts of the network, resulting in reduced flexibility for model-parallel learning. To verify this hypothesis, we conducted a more in-depth analysis using an expanded dataset and a larger network architecture, specifically training a speech recognition model on Librispeech. Our analysis confirmed that our initial findings were limited by the used dataset and network architecture, and in fact, various strategy-trained DNNs demonstrated minimal overlap in training regions, showing strong compatibility with model-parallel learning. Furthermore, Librispeech-based speech recognition models trained using Region Fusion overachieved the model-parallel learning compatibility of these strategies by 25% on average, indicating a promising approach for model-parallel learning. To facilitate this, we released our analysis code and models are now available via the MB-Merge repository.

The primary objective of damage detection systems for composite materials is to identify and pinpoint failures, but research can also focus on modifying their mechanical behavior. This study treats damage identification as a means to alter mechanical performance, allowing for real-time adjustment of stress distributions. A case is examined where a composite beam's bending stiffness profile is modified by accounting for pre-existing cracks. Data is collected using electrical impedance tomography and interpreted through Bayesian inference to generate accurate stiffness profiles. A novel approach is introduced to ensure the derived profile results in a predetermined damage location with minimal deviation. The algorithm involves adjusting the computed profile with a small random noise profile, selected using a fitness function that evaluates its impact on the stress distribution. The noise profile is chosen as one that maximizes the system's response to a given load. A practical example is provided, illustrating how the computed profile can be used to maintain a beam's integrity at a specific point despite damage.

We're excited to present our less intuitive model of generalized spin systems, characterized by stochastic interaction components. To our initial surprise, a purely logical application of this model inadvertently created an extensive macroscopic state in a specific subsystem, without any explicit design. Nonetheless, upon closer examination, we discovered that the model's parameters must meet extremely narrow constraints to achieve this effect, prompting a reevaluation of our conclusions.

A lucrative opportunity exists in the field of Lagrangian control, where model-free learning and tracker tracking can be achieved using a minimal amount of data and side information. This opportunity arises due to two factors: first, reinforcement learning algorithms rapidly converge when starting from a desirable initial position; second, neural network models can reliably predict an unknown trajectory based on just a single example. Combining these elements results in successful results with significantly less data, allowing for interesting experiments with extremely inefficient systems such as quadrupeds, airships, and vehicles lacking wheels. Notably, our approach succeeds with approximately ten successful trials for walking, approximately a thousand swimmings, and requires no data for reaching a target, instead proving effective with theoretical guarantees.

This study explores how a geometric approach to tensors benefits the representation of Euclidean spaces. We establish the linear equations using geometric quantities and derive the corresponding tensor transformation laws. Furthermore, this method allows for the automatic identification of fundamental tensor types, including contravariant, covariant, and mixed tensors of various orders. A key advantage of this method is its ability to perform tensor analysis without requiring the explicit use of the metric tensor. Instead, we can directly determine the contravariant and covariant basis vectors and express any tensor in terms of these basis vectors. For instance, the determination of the Riemann-Cristoffel symbols and the Ricci tensor can be performed without resorting to the metric tensor. A simplified algorithm has been developed to convert between different tensor representations using geometric quantities. Notably, a mutual relationship has been established between the Riemann tensor and six distinct forms of the Gaussian curvature, all with a potential application in general relativity.

Theoretical predictions for certain theoretical particles called NGLQPs offer a significant reduction in the expected duration these particles would take to disintegrate, with some models even predicting they could survive to reach terrestrial detectors. Despite this, the flavor-changing neutral current interactions that define these particles are not successfully captured by current disintegration searches. We propose new methods to identify these particles at linear colliders, which could lead to their detection through time-based projections in future experiments such as the International Linear Collider and CEPC.

The sudden shift to remote learning forced by the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the global education system, with the sudden transition to remote learning to COVID-19 pandemic forced a significant disruption to the global education system. To stay alive, many universities switched to remote learning, but this switch to remote learning to COVID-19 pandemic forced a significant disruption to the global education system. Switching to remote learning had varying effects on students' abilities to keep up with their studies, as some students benefited from the flexibility of remote learning, while others struggled with the lack of social interaction and physical separation from their families. To stay alive, some students even faced financial difficulties, with the sudden closure of universities leaving them without access to essential resources. Overall, the diverse impact of remote learning on students' ability to stay on track during the pandemic called for more research to determine the most effective ways to deliver remote education.

This research establishes the presence of Ward identities within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. We provide the fundamental basis vectors for primary correlations associated with three distinct spin values and a derived set of identities, then explicitly express the three-blob primary correlation in terms of Conformal Finite Mode (CFM) modes. Additionally, we outline the method to determine more intricate primary correlations by analyzing lower-complexity correlations and a derived function, offering an approach to isolate a specific component from an infinite series of possible components.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups belong to the class of bi-automatic groups,
implying that they are of type FP_2 as well as having virtually torsion-free
presentations with relations of degree at most 12. Consequently, we establish
that pure braided groups are of type FP_2.

Investigating the thermodynamics of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes in a scalar field theory reveals that certain singularities can be concealed from view by other horizons under specific conditions. A detailed analysis of how the entropy of these black holes changes with respect to their charges and the scalar field shows a pattern of decrease, followed by an increase, for an intermediate range, but consistently increases, or consistently decreases, in specific phases. This analysis indicates that the feeble cosmic censorship conjecture holds for a specific ratio of the charge to the horizon radius, but may fail in two distinct intervals. A quench process was also analyzed and its outcomes mirror those of an abrupt change in parameters. Furthermore, an investigation into thermal instabilities of these black holes in a canonical ensemble was conducted and its results are consistent with findings from a microcanonical ensemble analysis.

In this paper, we expand upon the foundational concepts of classical Zermelo-Fraenkel collection theory by incorporating paraconsistent and paracomplete logic into ZF. Specifically, we utilize the three-valued paraconsistent logic $B_3^p$ and the three-valued paracomplete logic $B_3^\vee$ as the underlying logic for modified versions of ZF, denoted as $ZF_{B_3^p}$ and $ZF_{B_3^\vee}$ respectively. Our analysis reveals that $ZF_{B_3^\vee}$ can be derived from $ZF_{B_3^p}$ through the application of Glivenko's Theorem, which in turn allows us to derive $ZF_{B_3^\vee}$ from classical ZF. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both $ZF_{B_3^p}$ and $ZF_{B_3^\vee}$ maintain equiconsistency with their classical counterparts.

Humans move by walking, but the complex brain mechanisms behind this movement remain poorly understood. Researchers have discovered that neurons fire in a distinct pattern while walking, forming two separate states known as walking states. In this study, we investigate the link between these brain activity patterns and the step rates at which humans walk. By analyzing data from implanted sensors in patients with epilepsy, we observe that step rates influence brain activity patterns in a specific way. Specifically, closer step rates resemble each other while greater distances between step rates have the potential to be used as a predictive measure. Notably, the link between walking states and step rates is not balanced, with the distance between brain activity patterns changing rapidly at low step rates but having a gradual change at higher rates. Understanding this relationship is crucial for uncovering how movements are coordinated and organized in the brain.

This paper proposes a new method to calculate entropy variations between two probability distributions, using the nested sampling technique. Our approach falls under the category of Kullback-Leibler entropy and offers benefits over traditional methods, particularly in handling high-dimensional scenarios. By leveraging nested sampling, we can decompose entropy calculation into manageable components, thereby avoiding direct computation of multi-variable quantities. A key advantage of this method is its applicability to discrete systems, where it provides consistent results. To compare and validate our approach, we conduct a study that outperforms common techniques such as histogram binning, neural networks, and dimensionality reduction methods. Our proposed method is then applied to calculating the entropy of mixed phases in a charged scalar field theory, yielding accurate and expected results for a range of parameters.

We extend the concept of right-angled Artin groups by adding a length function, making certain group elements behave like distinct points. This allows us to apply a method by Davis and Krop to analyze how these groups split into more complex structures. Our analysis uses a specific technique, the Tits geometric space, and leads to conclusions based on the properties of a subpart of the Tits space, following methods by Geiger and Rousseller.

In the field of time series analysis, research on graph-based methods for representing relationships in data is rapidly evolving. These methods, known as connectivity estimates, are essential in various areas of interest such as brain activity interpretation, stock market prediction, and crisis management. Current approaches fall short in efficiently handling large-scale data sets over extended periods, hindering their application to time-series information from multiple sources, such as local electroencephalogram (EEG) readings and high-frequency financial reports. To address this challenge, we developed a novel approach called Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity Estimation (DyECE), which leverages graph neural networks to create an adaptable and efficient graph structure that captures the dynamic relationships in the data. Our model excels in accurately capturing the evolving patterns in data over extended periods, outperforming existing methods such as Kluster-Transfer Learning (KTL) and Multi-task Transfer Learning (MTTL) in tasks such as data reconstruction, source classification, and data analysis, especially when working with large-scale data sets such as the International EEG dataset (IRecog) and high-frequency financial reports (ITrade).

Phylogenetic networks serve as comprehensive representations for the evolutionary histories of species, offering necessary and evolutionary historical information. Due to their complexity, phylogenetic networks are difficult to analyze, therefore researchers often utilize computational tools known as phylogenetic network generators to create them. Despite the prevalence of such generators, there is a lack of understanding regarding how they affect the resulting structure of the produced phylogenetic networks. This study is to examine the influence of different generation techniques on the topological features of a set of randomly generated phylogenetic networks, utilizing various metrics including reticularities, cycle lengths, and linear program values. We compare outputs from three distinct generation algorithms: random constructions, sequential formations, and the Phillips-Monte-Carlo method, then discuss how these techniques yield varying effects on the final phylogenetic network's structure.

Determining if a sample contains active, living organisms is a common lab practice that relies on microscopy. The traditional visual assessment through a microscope is being supplemented by audio analysis, as living cells often produce distinct sounds when interacting with one another. These biochemical communications can be facilitated through surfaces and can be captured for both auditory observation and visual confirmation. The primary objective of this project is to develop a straightforward, reproducible, user-friendly program that utilizes computational methods to analyze video footage and automatically detect cell or organism motion. The related research presented here presents the quantitative computational data employed to create this program, which is built using open-source, user-friendly tools and can be accessed via the accompanying GitHub repository.

Engineering designs are heavily dependent on acoustic emission testing, which utilizes a technique called the time reversal method to locate defects and generalize findings. The time reversal method requires solving multiple complex systems of linear equations, which can be computationally intensive. Researchers have discovered that iteratively solving these systems using higher-order methods, such as Kaczmarz and Davis-Kahan-Steinberg, leads to significant acceleration, resulting in a tenfold increase in processing time compared to conventional methods. The new algorithms have also been optimized for GPU implementation, further enhancing their efficiency and producing even faster results, which yield highly accurate location estimates when applied to acoustic emission test data.

We develop theoretical frameworks to investigate the concept of scattering systems, which can be quantified by the spatial distribution of light absorption or neutron energy deposition. Developing operators representing the probability of particle interaction, we analyze their specific outcomes and broader properties through spectral decomposition, thereby addressing the challenge of solving this class of problems. To tackle the problem of resonant enhancement in eigenchannels, specifically those associated with maximum absorption, we introduce appropriate metric and apply a variational approach to find optimal solutions. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated by calculating sum principles for electrolytic systems, espousal of variational concepts in scattering theory leads to significant simplifications, particularly the automatic satisfaction of normalization conditions.

Three-dimensional topological Anderson insulators, caused by random atomic-scale disorders, have been theoretically predicted. These insulators require a large number of different material components to model, which hinders their practical observation. Our model introduces the first prediction of topological Anderson insulators that can occur in alloys of two materials with distinct topological properties and conductance values, and we show that this phenomenon persists with increasing levels of random disorder. Additionally, our theoretical analysis encompasses both quasi-periodic and disordered settings, and it is supported by results from numerical simulations.

The n-dimensional cubical framework, often referred to as the domain of types, is a foundational structure for type theory. It employs a set of primitive constructs called cuts to define n-cubes based on lower-dimensional ones. Notably, these cuts represent fundamental transformations from (n-1)-cubes to n-cubes. To align with standard mathematical practices on n-cubes, we present an alternative definition of cuts and introduce new concepts, including the cut sum, cut pasting, and the cut projection. Then we demonstrate how n-cubes can be formed from (n-1)-cubes using these additional constructs.

We examine a specific scenario within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, where the Higgs boson's mass parameter is a real value derived from the product of two complex parameters, while other decay-suppressing combinations of these parameters are minimized. This "on-shell" approach is expanded upon by incorporating two additional mechanisms: neutralino mixing and top-quark chromatic effects. We derive analytical formulas for the Higgs boson's couplings to other particles, particularly focusing on its interactions with bottom quarks, charm quarks, and gluons. These formulas can be used to predict discrepancies in the Higgs boson's production methods, such as bottom-quark fusion and charm-quark fusion, as well as differences in its coupling to two gluons and two photons. Estimates of the required experimental precision to detect these discrepancies are provided. Furthermore, we determine the conditions on the on-shell parameters that would result in the standard relationship between these parameters and the Higgs boson's vacuum expectation depth, as well as the physical meaning of a specific on-shell parameter, which influences the Higgs boson's mass and determines which other parameters affect its interactions with quarks and bosons.
A new class of flexible, adaptive models has been created to test linearity in networks, and their performance has been verified through simulations and real data analysis.

Recent research has combined declarative knowledge graphs and machine learning by creating Deep Declarative Networks, which integrate knowledge graphs into neural networks. To enhance the framework of DDNs for diverse applications, this study focuses on two key areas: the internal structure and an specific application. Firstly, this study Intellificates the DDN framework, allowing for framework modifications and easy integration of new components, such as latent representations and prior probability, while ensuring consistency in overall integrality. Secondly, it examines a complex, multi-tiered challenge involving latent variables and cyclic dependencies that are often missed in standard DDN formulations. This study introduces an intricate framework and a novel algorithm to resolve this challenge, which is then applied to dataset completion. The results show significant improvements in performance compared to existing methods, particularly on the FB15k-2k dataset.

A dynamic and flexible membrane encloses cells, repositioning itself in response to internal cytosolic forces as they affect the behavior and movement of cells. This relocation is also responsible for the asymmetric distribution of molecules within the membrane, which in turn influences protein movement and cell behavior. To reiterate, the interplay between the membrane's ability to position itself, the movement of cells, and the distribution of molecules within the flat space constitutes a complex process that requires careful consideration. To better understand this process, a computational framework is proposed, integrating the visco-elastic properties of the membrane, the cell's ability to move, the transition between phases, a material that remembers its shape and the forces at play, along with a byproduct of the framework's repositioning, which is used to influence protein movement and cell behavior. As an added repositioning of the framework reuses the same principles to also model protein movement, relaying on the same framework to also cell behavior.

The primary function of a blockchain is to prevent double-spending and the creation of fake coins, with most cryptocurrencies lacking private information in their transaction history. To counter this, researchers have developed mixed coins and privacy-enhancing protocols, which, however, can introduce new risks by obscening the origin of funds and potentially facilitating the creation of currency trails for illegal activities. To investigate this, we analyzed Ethereum transactions involving two such protocols, CoinJoin and Zk-Snarks, after collecting a dataset of 790 suspected cases from 5 different exchanges. Our empirical research found that despite initially hiding transaction histories, the suspected activities examined could be traced back to their source, with a significant majority of cases (55 to 85 per cent) revealing a direct link to the original funds. Furthermore, we observed that exchanges frequently utilized mixed coins for illegal transactions, with up to 90 per cent of such cases (case duration <= 10 days) being successfully tracked, with shorter tracking periods corresponding to higher recovery rates (up to 93 per cent for 1 to 3 days). These findings highlight the need to develop more sophisticated anti-privacy techniques to effectively prevent the creation of such currency trails.

This research proposes a novel, learning-based approach to address the issue of fault tolerance in quantum computing. Specifically, we tackle the challenge of error correction in the surface code, which is a fundamental component for the future development of a functional quantum computer. Traditional methods to solve this problem involve intricate, time-consuming algorithms that require precise knowledge of the system's behavior. In contrast, our approach employs a neural network to simplify the problem into a series of basic decisions, enabling a faster solution. To enhance performance, we integrate past error patterns through a long short-term memory network, allowing our method to outperform the standard optimal approach and adapt to changes in error rates that the traditional method struggles with.

Precise timing measurements can potentially surpass the classical limit by utilizing entangled states, specifically, superpositions of entangled particles that can indicate their location simultaneously. This innovative approach could be realized in an isolated system comprising two coupled cavity quantum electrodynamics systems. In these systems, the Rabi oscillations between the cavities can be observed, and their duration can be measured to great precision using entangled states. Notably, the linear scaling of interaction strength in this model allows for improved signal-to-noise ratios, and the noise caused by unknown parameters can be reduced to a level comparable to that of independent particles. As a result, the quantum advantage in achieving precise timing measurements in this two-cavity system is maintained even in the presence of parametric noise.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron associations in 200 GeV/A $d$+$Au$ and $Au$+$Au$ collisions, featuring an enriched source of parton jets due to these interactions. By comparing hadron distributions associated with direct photons in these collisions, we can gain insights into the behavior of the quark-gluon plasma.
This paper extends research on the Smarandache multiplication of digits across various foundational numbers.

Network noise is an important concept to clarify when examining cloud computing performance. Virtualization technology is used to increase network resource utilization and overall system efficiency, but it also introduces hidden variability that can affect how applications function. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of network noise caused by the shared nature of virtualized environments. Specifically, it examines the sources of this noise, its characteristics, and its effects on application scalability. To gather necessary data for this study, it uses a combination of live cloud environment monitoring and controlled laboratory testing. The findings it presents are relevant to cloud architects and scalability planning specialists, offering insights into how to design and scale applications to maximize performance and reliability.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has been extensively studied. It is particularly useful to study the context of learning through a decentralized approach in a network. In a wireless network context, this can be done by allowing local decision-makers to learn from their own experiences and communicate this learning to others, ultimately making them more efficient. A key challenge here is ensuring that the learning algorithm doesn't rely heavily on the amount of data that is shared. We present a novel algorithm for this decentralized learning process, which involves context. This algorithm guarantees that the losses incurred are nearly optimal, growing at a rate of O(log^2 T)/sh, where T represents the number of steps, and 's' denotes the amount of data that is shared per step. We prove a lower bound for the losses in this context, which shows that our algorithm performs well and is efficient. Numerical experiments demonstrate the performance of our algorithm, and we observe the conditions under which it performs optimally, and the conditions under which it is inefficient, and the conditions under which it is inefficient.

Over the past year, remote working via videoconferencing and email has risen dramatically among UK companies. This significant shift is particularly relevant to organizations utilizing the Scrum framework for managing projects, given its already established reliance on remote collaboration. Our comprehensive research study examined how working from home affects the effectiveness of organizations implementing Scrum, by combining quantitative and qualitative approaches to work together seamlessly. Initially, we gathered data through a large-scale online survey involving 1451 participants, which was followed by in-depth interviews with 14 additional participants to deepen our understanding of working from home within Scrum projects. Our research findings were presented through both statistical analysis and thematic exploration to ensure a cohesive approach to evidence gathering. Ultimately, our results show that teams working from home may encounter difficulties with meeting attendance, but these challenges can be overcome with meeting facilitation techniques, clear communication, meeting attendance, and the use of visual management tools like Kanban boards, which can be easily adapted to working from home environments, as indicated by our research using a rigorous method known as HOSMEM.

We appreciate the interest shown by readers. In our response, we address the concerns raised by the commentators. Specifically, we clarify the distinction between the objectives set by Muñana-Fernández et al. and those by Dustin Chambers in their respective works. Furthermore, we answer the questions posed by the commentators, address any misunderstandings, and provide additional details to clarify our approach.

This study examines the influence of event shape fluctuations and initial state asymmetry on the elliptic flow $v_2$ and elliptic flow-to-spectra ratio $v_2/n$ in lead-lead collisions at $\sqrt{s_\rm{NN}} = 2.76$ TeV, focusing on midrapidity data and transverse momentum ranges between 2 and 8 GeV/$c$. By analyzing plane distribution spectra and simulating initial state asymmetry's impact using the IP-Glauber model, researchers found that fluctuations significantly affect $v_2$ and $v_2/n$ but have minimal impact on integrated spectra and $v_2/n$ at high $n$. To investigate this effect, the event-shape-Engineering (ESE) method was employed, selecting sorted spectra for events with more (more ESE events) or fewer (less ESE events than average) asymmetry. Comparing these selected spectra to average (integrated) spectra revealed that more (less) events exhibit a more (less) pronounced $v_2$ structure, with the difference increasing as $n$ decreases, particularly in mid-$n$ ranges, resulting in a nearly identical $v_2/n$ structure. Based on the form of the $v_2$ structure, the possible causes of the event-shape fluctuation's impact were analyzed, including more chaotic (less ordered) matter motion (more disordered) than the opposite (less dis

This paper proposes novel quaternion-valued functions linked to the Logarithmic Correlator in the LCST domain, introducing two types of energy constraints to identify specific properties. These properties, when combined with an inequality inequality derivation, facilitate the uniqueness of a function through its logarithmic correlator and the location of its energy concentration centers. Furthermore, the paper discusses the application of the Hermitian property of the Logarithmic Correlator in the LCST domain and proposes additional constraints to derive uniqueness theorems for a function by its logarithmic correlator and support of its maximum modulus within the LCST domain, all of which leverage the discriminant property of a matrix.

This research builds upon the previously discovered optimal GDoF power control method for interference networks, which involves assigning positive real-valued power levels to meet a total of $K$ power levels, resulting in an extremal GDoF benefit of $\Theta(K^{2/3})$ over using binary power control. We refine this outcome to $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$, representing a more accurate characterization of the significant gain achievable through optimal power control. Moreover, we provide achievable schemes that verify the character of our benefit as well as lower bounds that match our upper bounds for the extremal gDoF benefit of optimal power control.

A novel, efficient strategy has been devised to optimize the collision time in three-dimensional, multiple-resolved simulations, particularly for scenarios involving discharging processes. The method modifies the collision time based on the numerical integration scheme's accuracy, ultimately increasing computational efficiency. By selectively updating the collision time for each particle, the new method outperforms traditional fixed-time approaches, demonstrating significant gains in computational performance for complex scenarios such as free-falling processes.

This article provides the following proof: for any positive integer $n$, there exist positive whole numbers $a$ and $b$ such that the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ holds true, specifically with $a=b=7^{\lfloor n/3 \rfloor}$ and $7^{r} | \binom{2\cdot 7^{ \lfloor n/3 \rfloor } }{ 7^{\lfloor (n+2)/3 \rfloor} }$, where $r$ equals the remainder when $n$ is divided by three.

This paper is interested in creating a mathematical model for a one-legged hopping robot moving on a surface that deforms under pressure. We derived a model based on torque-controlled joints, then examined how the robot's mass and friction resistance affect its movement. A simulation was performed to compare predicted mass changes with actual data during a hop, and it confirmed the model's accuracy. Furthermore, the effect of adding rotational inertia to the leg was explored, and a method to improve the model's performance was proposed.

QCD sum rules effectively predict the flexibility of the meson's average spatial extent, which is related to its radial distribution function. Our new method calculates the flexibility of mesons, such as pions, by using flexible sums of QCD in a consistent framework, considering both meson ground and first excited states. This method finds the point of stability in a meson's flexibility prediction, which is indicative of its physical behavior. Similarly, we determine the flexibility of vector mesons, such as the $\rho$-meson, by flexibly summing the hadronic and QCD representations of their associated properties.
